fuentes/palido-fuego/resumen.texto: Novel presented as a 999-line poem by the fictional John Shade, with a foreword, an extensive commentary and an index by his neighbor and colleague Charles Kinbote, who turns the poem into an account of his supposed exile as king of Zembla. The story takes place in the fictional college town of New Wye, in the United States, between February and October 1959. Nabokov wrote it in 1960 and 1961, beginning it in Nice and finishing it in Montreux. It was published in 1962.

fuentes/palido-fuego/por_que_importa.texto: It is cited as an example of metafiction and as an analogical precursor of hypertext fiction. It has generated an extensive critical literature and many interpretations.

fuentes/la-defensa-nabokov/resumen.texto: Nabokov's third novel, about Luzhin, a withdrawn and obsessive child chess prodigy whose life falls apart when he tries to apply a chess defense to reality. It appeared in 1929 and 1930 in the Russian émigré magazine Sovremennye zapiski, and in book form in Berlin from the publisher Slovo. Nabokov translated it into English with Michael Scammell in 1964, under the title The Defense.

fuentes/la-defensa-nabokov/por_que_impor.texto: It was written in exile, in Russian, before Nabokov switched to English.

fuentes/la-biblioteca-de-babel/resumen.texto: Story about a universe in the form of an immense library, made of identical hexagonal galleries containing all possible books of a certain format and a combination of twenty-five symbols. Its inhabitants seek meaning in that almost infinite collection. It was published in 1941 in the book The Garden of Forking Paths, and later included in Ficciones (1944). Earlier, in 1939, Borges had written the essay “The Total Library.”

fuentes/la-biblioteca-de-babel/por_que_i.texto: It is one of Borges's most commented stories. It has been used to think about infinity, information and chance; for example, the space of possible protein sequences has been compared to that library.

fuentes/mil-grullas/resumen.texto: Novel centered on the tea ceremony. Kikuji, a Tokyo office worker, attends the classes of the teacher Chikako Kurimoto, a former lover of his father, and becomes involved with Mrs. Ota, another former lover of his father, and later with Mrs. Ota's daughter. It was serialized from 1949 to 1951 and published as a book in 1952. In 1953 a third part was mentioned, but the story that would have returned to the protagonist was left unfinished.

fuentes/mil-grullas/por_que_importa.texto: It uses the tea ceremony and its objects as the thread of the story. Kawabata rejected readings of it as an evocation of the beauty of the tea ceremony and described it as “a negative work,” a warning against the vulgarity into which he had fallen. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1968.

fuentes/la-guerra-no-tiene-rostro-de-muj.texto: Documentary book with accounts of women who took part in World War II in the Red Army in various roles. Alexievich wrote it in 1983 based on interviews; it appeared in the magazine Oktyabr in early 1984 and as a book in 1985. Soviet censorship, or the author herself, removed passages that accused it of pacifism and naturalism and of diminishing the heroism of the Soviet woman; later editions restored many of them. It is the first book of the cycle “Voices from Utopia.”
It is Alexievich's first published book and established her method of gathering individual voices. It is the first part of the cycle to which Voices from Chernobyl also belongs.

fuentes/por-quien-doblan-las-campanas/re.texto: Novel about Robert Jordan, an American volunteer, formerly a Spanish teacher and an explosives expert, who fights with a Republican guerrilla band in the Guadarrama mountains during the Spanish Civil War and receives orders to blow up a bridge before the Segovia offensive, at the end of May 1937. Hemingway wrote it in 1939 between Havana, Key West and Idaho, finished it in July 1940 in New York, and Scribner's published it on 21 October 1940, shortly after the end of the war. The title comes from a meditation by the poet John Donne, from 1624.

fuentes/por-quien-doblan-las-campanas/po.texto: It is Hemingway's novel about the Spanish Civil War, which he covered as a correspondent. It portrays the Republican side with its internal tensions; in chapter 10, Pilar recounts the execution of supporters of the rebel side in her town, a scene based on what happened in Ronda in 1936, although Hemingway said in 1954 that he had invented it. It came out before the United States had entered World War II.

fuentes/adios-a-las-armas/resumen.texto: Novel narrated in the first person by Frederic Henry, an American lieutenant in the ambulance corps of the Italian army during World War I, who falls in love with the English nurse Catherine Barkley; it includes the Italian retreat after the battle of Caporetto. Hemingway, who had been a volunteer ambulance driver in Italy, wrote parts of it in Piggott, Arkansas, and Mission Hills, Kansas. It was serialized in Scribner's Magazine between May and October 1929 and published as a book on 27 September 1929; in Italy it could not be published until 1948, because the fascist regime judged it harmful to the honor of the armed forces.

fuentes/adios-a-las-armas/por_que_import.texto: It was Hemingway's first major bestseller and secured his place among American modern novelists; it has been called the principal American novel about World War I.

fuentes/adios-a-las-armas/leer.0.titulo.texto: English text on Wikisource (public domain in the United States since 2025)

fuentes/fiesta-hemingway/escrita.lugar.texto: Paris (begun in Valencia; revised in Schruns)

fuentes/fiesta-hemingway/resumen.texto: Hemingway's first full-length novel. It follows a group of American and British expatriates who travel from Paris to the San Fermín festival in Pamplona, where they watch the running of the bulls and the bullfights. Jake Barnes, a journalist wounded in the war, and the divorcée Brett Ashley are at the center of the story, a roman à clef based on people from Hemingway's circle and on his 1925 trip to Spain. He finished the draft on September 21, 1925, revised it thoroughly from December in Schruns (Austria), and Scribner's published it on October 22, 1926; in London it came out in 1927 under the title Fiesta, the one used in the United Kingdom.

fuentes/fiesta-hemingway/por_que_importa.texto: It presents the “lost generation” of the interwar years, which Hemingway describes as resilient and not merely damaged by the war. It shows his spare style and the “theory of the iceberg,” and it has remained in print since its publication.

fuentes/fiesta-hemingway/leer.0.titulo.texto: English text on Wikisource (public domain in the United States)

fuentes/tener-y-no-tener/resumen.texto: Novel about Harry Morgan, captain of a fishing boat from Key West (Florida) who, ruined by a client who does not pay him, turns to smuggling between Cuba and Florida during the Great Depression. It grew out of two earlier stories, “One Trip Across” (Cosmopolitan, 1934) and “The Tradesman's Return” (Esquire, 1936), which form its first chapters, and out of a novella written afterward; several characters narrate it. Hemingway wrote it intermittently between 1935 and 1937, revised it during his trips to Spain during the Spanish Civil War, and Scribner's published it on October 15, 1937.

fuentes/tener-y-no-tener/por_que_importa.texto: It is his fourth novel and the second set in the United States; it contrasts the poor of Key West with the owners of yachts. The biographer Jeffrey Meyers describes it as strongly influenced by the Marxism to which Hemingway was exposed through his support for the Republicans in Spain.

fuentes/paris-era-una-fiesta/resumen.texto: Memoir about the 1920s in Paris, when Hemingway was a journalist and a poor expatriate writer. It recounts his first marriage, to Hadley Richardson, and his dealings with figures of the Lost Generation such as Sylvia Beach, Gertrude Stein, Ezra Pound, Ford Madox Ford, James Joyce and F. Scott Fitzgerald. According to the note by his widow, Mary Hemingway, he began it in Cuba in the autumn of 1957, worked on it in Ketchum (Idaho), and finished it in Cuba in the spring of 1960; she edited it, and it was published posthumously in 1964. In 2009 a “restored edition” prepared by his grandson Seán Hemingway appeared.

fuentes/paris-era-una-fiesta/por_que_imp.texto: There is debate over which edition reflects Hemingway's wishes: A. E. Hotchner maintained that the 1964 edition is the one he wanted, while Gerry Brenner documented Mary Hemingway's corrections in 1982 and judged some of them ill-advised.

fuentes/las-nieves-del-kilimanjaro/resum.texto: Short story about Harry, a writer who dies of gangrene during a safari in Africa, stranded with his wife Helen at a camp because a bearing on the truck burned out. While he waits, he reviews his life and the stories he never wrote. It opens with a passage about Kilimanjaro and a leopard frozen near its summit. It was published in August 1936 in Esquire magazine and reissued in 1938 in the volume The Fifth Column and the First Forty-Nine Stories.

fuentes/las-nieves-del-kilimanjaro/por_q.texto: It is one of Hemingway's most widely read stories and was adapted to film in 1952, with Gregory Peck.

fuentes/al-otro-lado-del-rio-y-entre-los.texto: Across the River and into the Trees
Finca Vigía, Cuba (also Cortina d'Ampezzo, Paris and Venice)

Novel about the American colonel Richard Cantwell, fifty years old and with a terminal heart condition, who hunts ducks near Venice and, in a long flashback, recalls his service on the Italian front of World War I and his romance with a young Venetian woman, Renata. Hemingway wrote it between 1949 and 1950 in Cortina d'Ampezzo, Cuba, Paris and Venice; Cosmopolitan serialized it from February to June 1950, and Scribner's published it as a book on September 7, 1950. The title comes from the last words of the Confederate general Stonewall Jackson.
It was the first Hemingway novel to receive negative reviews, and his first book since For Whom the Bell Tolls (1940).

fuentes/el-amor-en-los-tiempos-del-coler.texto: Love in the Time of Cholera

Novel about Florentino Ariza and Fermina Daza, who fall in love as young people and are separated when her father prevents the match; Fermina marries the physician Juvenal Urbino, and Florentino pledges his love to her for more than fifty years, until Urbino dies. The city is never named and combines features of Cartagena and Barranquilla. It was published in 1985, three years after its author's Nobel Prize, and is said to have been inspired by the courtship of García Márquez's parents.
Together with Chronicle of a Death Foretold and Of Love and Other Demons, it forms what has been called García Márquez's “love triptych.”

fuentes/el-coronel-no-tiene-quien-le-esc.texto: No One Writes to the Colonel

Novella about a retired colonel, a veteran of the Thousand Days' War, who for about fifteen years has been waiting for the pension he was promised, and who lives with his asthmatic wife in a town under martial law during the years of La Violencia in Colombia; his only hope is a fighting cock inherited from his dead son. García Márquez wrote it between 1956 and 1957 in Paris, at the Hôtel des Trois Collèges; it appeared in 1958 in the magazine Mito (no. 19) and as a book in 1961.

García Márquez considered it his best book and said he had to write One Hundred Years of Solitude for people to read No One Writes to the Colonel. It is more realistic than his later works and shows the poverty and censorship of the period.

fuentes/el-otono-del-patriarca/resumen.texto: Political novel about the life of an eternal dictator in a fictional country on the Caribbean coast, divided into six sections that retell the same story of unlimited power. García Márquez said it was a “poem on the loneliness of power” and blended traits of real rulers, such as Gustavo Rojas Pinilla, Francisco Franco, François Duvalier and Juan Vicente Gómez. He wrote it in Barcelona and it was published in 1975.

fuentes/el-otono-del-patriarca/por_que_i.texto: It is one of the dictator novels of Latin American literature. In 1975 it was the best-selling book in Spain, according to the Instituto Español del Libro.

fuentes/cronica-de-una-muerte-anunciada/.texto: Novella that, in the form of a pseudo-journalistic reconstruction, recounts the murder of Santiago Nasar by the Vicario twins, who announced what they were going to do without anyone stopping them. It was inspired by a real event: on January 22, 1951, in Sucre, Miguel Reyes Palencia returned his wife, Margarita Chica Salas, to her family's home because she was not a virgin, and her brother Víctor killed Cayetano Gentile Chimeno. It was published in 1981.
It mixes the form of journalism with fiction and, together with Love in the Time of Cholera and Of Love and Other Demons, forms a love triptych.

fuentes/memoria-de-mis-putas-tristes/res.texto: Novella narrated in the first person by a journalist who has just turned ninety and seeks to spend the night with a fourteen-year-old girl who sells her virginity to help her family. Instead of sex, he discovers love for the first time in his life. It was published in Spanish in 2004, was the last novel García Márquez published in his lifetime, and had a film adaptation in 2012.

fuentes/memoria-de-mis-putas-tristes/por.texto: It was his first novel in ten years, since Of Love and Other Demons, and critics were divided: John Updike called it a “velvety pleasure to read, though somewhat unpleasant to contemplate,” and Michiko Kakutani, in The New York Times, called it “a listless narrative exercise.” It was banned in Iran after selling 5,000 copies.

fuentes/el-general-en-su-laberinto/resum.texto: Semi-fictional historical novel about the last seven months of Simón Bolívar, the Liberator. It recounts his journey from Bogotá to the Caribbean coast of Colombia, beginning on May 8, 1830, in an attempt to leave South America and go into exile in Europe. García Márquez decided to write it after reading an unfinished novel by his friend Álvaro Mutis about Bolívar's journey along the Magdalena River. It was published in 1989 simultaneously in Argentina, Colombia, Mexico and Spain.

fuentes/el-general-en-su-laberinto/por_q.texto: It is García Márquez's novel built around a real historical figure, the Liberator, on the last journey of his life.

fuentes/del-amor-y-otros-demonios/resume.texto: Novel set in Cartagena de Indias in the eighteenth century. Sierva María, the twelve-year-old daughter of a marquis, is bitten by a rabid dog; she does not seem to have been infected, but her family hands her over to a convent. In the prologue García Márquez recounts that the story was born when he witnessed the opening of some tombs and saw the tomb of a girl with hair twenty-two meters long. It was published in Spanish in 1994 and in English in 1995.

fuentes/del-amor-y-otros-demonios/por_qu.texto: It is the third book of what has been called a love triptych, together with Chronicle of a Death Foretold and Love in the Time of Cholera. In 2008 the composer Péter Eötvös premiered an opera based on it.

fuentes/totem-y-tabu/resumen.texto: Book in which Freud applies psychoanalysis to anthropology, archaeology and the history of religion, and compares the mental life of peoples called “savages” with that of neurotics. It brings together four essays first published in the journal Imago in 1912 and 1913: “The Horror of Incest,” “Taboo and the Ambivalence of Feelings,” “Animism, Magic and the Omnipotence of Thoughts” and “The Return of Totemism in Childhood.” It uses the concepts of projection and ambivalence, which he had developed with neurotic patients in Vienna, to explain the link between taboo and totemism.

fuentes/totem-y-tabu/por_que_importa.texto: Its theses were rejected by anthropology: the anthropologist Alfred Kroeber criticized them in 1920 and again in 1952, and Peter Farb wrote that by about 1968 anthropologists regarded them as discredited. Even so, René Girard took up its idea of a collective murder at the origin of society.

fuentes/totem-y-tabu/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation by A. A. Brill (1918) on Wikisource

fuentes/el-malestar-en-la-cultura/resume.texto: Essay in which Freud studies the clash between the desire for individuality and the demands of society, and the fundamental tensions between civilization and the individual. He wrote it in 1929, eleven years after the end of World War I, and it was published in German in 1930 in Vienna. It takes up ideas from The Future of an Illusion (1927), where he had criticized organized religion as a collective neurosis.

fuentes/el-malestar-en-la-cultura/por_qu.texto: The historian Peter Gay described it in 1989 as one of the most influential and most studied books of modern psychology. Together with Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego (1921), it is the most important of Freud's works on social psychology.

fuentes/el-malestar-en-la-cultura/leer.0.texto: English translation on Project Gutenberg (public domain in the United States)

fuentes/tres-ensayos-sobre-teoria-sexual.texto: Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality

Work in which Freud sets out his theory of sexuality and its relation to childhood, in three parts: sexual aberrations, infantile sexuality, and puberty. In the first he distinguishes the sexual object from the sexual aim and notes that deviations from the norm can occur in either. The 1905 edition proposes an autoerotic theory of sexual development, without the Oedipus complex; in the later editions, over twenty years, Freud rewrote and expanded it from some 80 to some 120 pages.
Together with The Interpretation of Dreams, it is one of Freud's most important contributions, and it placed infantile sexuality at the center of psychoanalysis.
English translation by A. A. Brill (1910) on Wikisource

fuentes/el-porvenir-de-una-ilusion/resum.texto: Essay in which Freud treats the origins, development and future of religion, and analyzes it as an illusion: a belief sustained by desire, which Freud distinguishes from error and which is not necessarily false, although he considers religious doctrines improbable. He defines religion as an illusion, made up of dogmas that say something one has not discovered for oneself and that demand to be believed.

fuentes/el-porvenir-de-una-ilusion/por_q.texto: It is his analysis of religion as a collective neurosis, an idea he took up again in Civilization and Its Discontents (1930).

fuentes/el-porvenir-de-una-ilusion/leer..texto: English translation on Project Gutenberg (public domain in the United States)

fuentes/moises-y-la-religion-monoteista/.texto: Book of three essays on the origins of monotheism, written between 1934 and 1938 and first published as a book by Allert de Lange, in Amsterdam, in 1939; the first two had appeared in 1937 and the third in 1938. Freud proposes that Moses was an Egyptian follower of the monotheism of Akhenaten and not a Hebrew raised at court, as the Book of Exodus tells, and that the Israelites killed him and the guilt for that crime shaped the Jewish religion. He wrote the third part in London, where he arrived after the Nazi annexation of Austria; in a letter to Arnold Zweig dated June 28, 1938, he said he was working on it.

It is Freud's last original work, published a few months before his death, and it surprised many readers with its thesis of an Egyptian Moses. It is his second work on Moses, after “The Moses of Michelangelo” (1914).
German text “Der Mann Moses und die monotheistische Religion” (Projekt Gutenberg-DE)

fuentes/la-muerte-en-venecia/resumen.texto: Novella about Gustav von Aschenbach, an acclaimed writer who travels to Venice, becomes obsessed with the Polish adolescent Tadzio, and dies in a cholera epidemic. It draws on Mann's stay in Venice in the summer of 1911, during that year's cholera epidemic; Tadzio is said to have been based on a boy named Władzio whom Mann observed there, and the death of Gustav Mahler in Vienna in May 1911 also occupied his thoughts. It came out in 1912 in a limited edition from Hyperion-Verlag and in serial form in Die neue Rundschau, and in a commercial Fischer edition in 1913.

fuentes/la-muerte-en-venecia/por_que_imp.texto: Together with The Magic Mountain and Buddenbrooks, it is counted among Mann's best-known works; its plot is an aesthetic reflection on passion, ideal love and beauty.

fuentes/la-muerte-en-venecia/leer.1.titu.texto: German text “Der Tod in Venedig” (Projekt Gutenberg-DE)

fuentes/doktor-faustus/resumen.texto: Novel that retells the legend of Faust in Germany in the first half of the twentieth century. The narrator, Serenus Zeitblom, writes between 1943 and 1946 the life of his childhood friend, the fictional composer Adrian Leverkühn, who deliberately contracts syphilis to make a pact with the devil that gives him creative genius, and who falls into madness until his death. His life runs in parallel with the Germany that leads to Nazism. Mann began it in 1943 and it was published in 1947; in 1949 he published his own account of how the novel came about.

fuentes/doktor-faustus/por_que_importa.texto: Mann wrote it in exile, in Los Angeles, and among its themes is the intellectual decline of Germany in the years before World War II. Schoenberg, who lived nearby, was annoyed because Leverkühn used his twelve-tone technique without his consent, and later editions carry a note by Mann acknowledging this.

fuentes/tonio-kroger/resumen.texto: Novella that follows the life of a man from his schooldays to adulthood. The son of a merchant from northern Germany and of a “southern” mother with artistic talent, Tonio feels an unbridgeable contrast between art and the bourgeoisie. It has autobiographical traits: his admiration for his schoolmate Hans Hansen was based, according to a letter by Mann, on the feeling he had for his Lübeck schoolmate Armin Martens. He wrote it around 1900–1902 (other chronologies place it in early 1901) and it was published in 1903.

fuentes/tonio-kroger/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of Mann's first novellas and deals with the artist facing the bourgeois world, a theme he returned to.

fuentes/jose-y-sus-hermanos/resumen.texto: Tetralogy that retells the stories of Genesis (chapters 27 to 50), from Jacob to Joseph, within the historical setting of the Amarna period. It consists of The Tales of Jacob (December 1926 to October 1930), The Young Joseph (January 1931 to June 1932), Joseph in Egypt (July 1932 to August 1936) and Joseph the Provider (August 1940 to January 1943). S. Fischer in Berlin published the first two volumes (1933 and 1934); Joseph in Egypt came out in Vienna in 1936 and Joseph the Provider in Stockholm in 1943, both from the exile publisher Bermann-Fischer. Mann finished the last one in California.

fuentes/jose-y-sus-hermanos/por_que_impo.texto: It is Mann's most voluminous work, written over sixteen years, and he considered it his best. His presentation of the ancient Near East and the origins of Judaism was influenced by Alfred Jeremias and Dmitry Merezhkovsky.

fuentes/jose-y-sus-hermanos/leer.0.titul.texto: German text, first volume “Die Geschichten Jaakobs” (Projekt Gutenberg-DE)

fuentes/jose-y-sus-hermanos/leer.1.titul.texto: German text, second volume “Der junge Joseph” (Projekt Gutenberg-DE)

fuentes/al-este-del-eden/resumen.texto: Family saga of the Trasks and the Hamiltons in the Salinas Valley of California, from the Civil War to World War I. Viking Press published it in September 1952, and it quickly reached the top of the bestseller lists. Steinbeck considered it his greatest work: “It has everything I have been able to learn about my craft in all these years.”

fuentes/al-este-del-eden/por_que_importa.texto: Its popularity grew again in 2003, when Oprah Winfrey's book club chose it. It tells the story of two families from the author's home region.

fuentes/la-perla-steinbeck/resumen.texto: Novella about Kino, a pearl diver, which explores greed, defiance of social norms and evil. Steinbeck began it in 1944 as a film script, published it as a story, “The Pearl of the World,” in Woman's Home Companion in December 1945, and expanded it into a novella in 1947 (Viking Press). It is inspired by a Mexican folk tale from La Paz, Baja California, which he had mentioned in The Sea of Cortez (1940), the book written with marine biologist Ed Ricketts.

fuentes/la-perla-steinbeck/por_que_impor.texto: It is widely used in American schools and is sometimes considered a parable. Steinbeck wrote that he wanted to address human greed, materialism and the inherent worth of things.

fuentes/tortilla-flat/resumen.texto: Picaresque novel set in Monterey (California), about a group of “paisanos” of Mexican, Native American and Spanish descent who live off wine and idleness in the days after World War I. The work presents them as a caricature of the Knights of the Round Table. It was published in 1935, adapted for the stage in 1938 and for film in 1942.

fuentes/tortilla-flat/por_que_importa.texto: It was Steinbeck's first clear success with critics and sales. He returned to some of the Monterey vagrants in Cannery Row (1945).

fuentes/una-habitacion-propia/resumen.texto: Extended essay divided into six chapters, based on two lectures Woolf gave in October 1928 at two women's colleges at Cambridge, Newnham and Girton. It deals with women and writing and argues that “a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction.” It was published on October 24, 1929. It mentions the obscenity trial against Radclyffe Hall's novel The Well of Loneliness (1928).

fuentes/una-habitacion-propia/por_que_im.texto: It brings together Woolf's arguments on women and writing, which are widely cited in feminist literary criticism. Before publishing it, Woolf noted in her diary that she expected to be accused of feminism.

fuentes/una-habitacion-propia/leer.0.tit.texto: 1929 Hogarth Press edition in English, on Wikisource

fuentes/orlando/resumen.texto: Novel published on October 11, 1928 by the Woolfs' press, Hogarth Press, inspired by the turbulent family history of the aristocratic poet and novelist Vita Sackville-West, Woolf's friend and lover. It recounts the adventures of a poet who is born a male nobleman in the reign of Elizabeth I, becomes a woman, and lives for centuries, up to the day of publication. It is a history of English literature in satirical form.

fuentes/orlando/por_que_importa.texto: Sackville-West's son, Nigel Nicolson, wrote that Vita's effect on Virginia is all in Orlando, “the longest and most charming love letter in literature.”

fuentes/orlando/leer.0.titulo.texto: English text on Wikisource (public domain in the United States)

fuentes/las-olas/resumen.texto: Novel published on October 8, 1931, made up of soliloquies by six characters, Bernard, Susan, Rhoda, Neville, Jinny and Louis, whom it follows from childhood to adulthood. Between the soliloquies come nine brief third-person interludes describing a coastal scene at different moments of a day, from sunrise to sunset. Percival, a seventh character, appears in the soliloquies but never speaks. In her diary, Woolf noted that the six were not separate “characters” but facets of a single consciousness.

fuentes/las-olas/por_que_importa.texto: It is considered the culmination of her experimental lyrical technique. In a 2015 BBC poll it ranked 16th among the best British novels.

fuentes/al-faro/resumen.texto: Novel about the Ramsay family and their visits to their summer home on the Isle of Skye, in the Scottish Hebrides, between 1910 and 1920. The plot counts for less than philosophical introspection: there is almost no dialogue or direct action, and almost everything is told through thoughts and observations, from the viewpoints of several characters. Hogarth Press, the publishing house of Virginia and Leonard Woolf, published it on May 5, 1927. Woolf began writing it partly to deal with unresolved matters with her parents, and the plot has many parallels with her own life.

fuentes/al-faro/por_que_importa.texto: It continues and extends the tradition of modernist novelists such as Proust and Joyce, and it is a frequently cited example of the technique of multiple focalization.

fuentes/la-casa-de-bernarda-alba/resumen.texto: Drama in three acts, subtitled “a drama of women in the villages of Spain,” about Bernarda Alba, who is widowed for the second time at sixty. It was Lorca's last play, finished on June 19, 1936, two months before his murder during the Spanish Civil War. It premiered on March 8, 1945, at the Teatro Avenida in Buenos Aires, thanks to the initiative of the actress Margarita Xirgu, and was published that same year.

fuentes/la-casa-de-bernarda-alba/por_que.texto: It is usually grouped with Blood Wedding and Yerma as the “rural trilogy,” although Lorca did not include it in his planned “trilogy of the Spanish land,” which was left unfinished.

fuentes/bodas-de-sangre/resumen.texto: Tragedy in verse and prose set in rural Spain, which Lorca wrote around 1931–1932. It premiered at the Teatro Beatriz in Madrid on March 8, 1933, and that same year in Buenos Aires. It is linked to the Níjar (Almería) crime of July 22, 1928, which Lorca learned about from the press.

fuentes/bodas-de-sangre/por_que_importa.texto: It is usually grouped with Yerma and The House of Bernarda Alba as Lorca's “rural trilogy,” although he projected it as a “trilogy of the Spanish land” that he never completed.

fuentes/yerma/resumen.texto: Play that Lorca called a “tragic poem,” written in 1934 and premiered that year, on December 29, at the Teatro Español in Madrid. It tells the story of a childless woman in rural Spain whose desire to become a mother becomes an obsession that ends in a crime. It is divided into three acts of two scenes each.

fuentes/yerma/por_que_importa.texto: Together with Blood Wedding and The House of Bernarda Alba, it forms Lorca's “rural trilogy,” a name given to it by commentators.

fuentes/la-broma/resumen.texto: Milan Kundera's first novel, published in 1967. It tells how a private joke by a student, Ludvik Jahn, ruins his life: he is expelled from school and from the Communist Party for his irreverence. The stories of his lovers and friends intertwine with the role of folk traditions and religion in communist Czechoslovakia. The manuscript was finished in Prague in 1965, but the censors' complaints delayed its publication until 1967.

fuentes/la-broma/por_que_importa.texto: It was read as a denunciation of Stalinism; Kundera rejected that reading in the 1982 preface to the English edition (“Spare me your Stalinism, please. The Joke is a love story”). After the Soviet invasion of 1968, Kundera was placed on blacklists.

fuentes/la-vida-esta-en-otra-parte/resum.texto: Novel that Kundera finished in 1969, in Bohemia, and first published in French in 1973 (La vie est ailleurs). It tells the story of Jaromil, a young poet, and his mother, who cling to each other while he seeks artistic fame and the revolution advances at the expense of his most intimate relationships, in Czechoslovakia before, during and after World War II. The French publisher Claude Gallimard visited Kundera in Prague and took the manuscript to France, where Gallimard published it.

fuentes/la-vida-esta-en-otra-parte/por_q.texto: It appeared first in French, after the manuscript had left Czechoslovakia.

fuentes/el-libro-de-la-risa-y-el-olvido/.texto: The Book of Laughter and Forgetting

Novel made up of seven separate narratives linked by common themes, which considers how forgetting operates in history, in politics and in life. It contains elements of magical realism. Kundera finished it in 1978 and it was published in France in 1979 (Le Livre du rire et de l'oubli); the Czech edition was issued in April 1981 by the exile publisher 68 Publishers, of Toronto. In it he describes a photograph of February 21, 1948, in which Vladimír Clementis stands beside Klement Gottwald, and how state propaganda erased him from that photo after accusing him in 1950, an example that underscores the theme of forgetting.
It is Kundera's novel of exile, written after the Soviet occupation of 1968, which it refers to in one of its parts.

fuentes/sin-blanca-en-paris-y-londres/ti.texto: Down and Out in Paris and London

fuentes/sin-blanca-en-paris-y-londres/re.texto: Orwell's first full-length book, published on January 9, 1933: a memoir in two parts about poverty in Paris and London. The first recounts his almost destitute life in the Latin Quarter, where he moved in the spring of 1928, and his occasional work in restaurant kitchens; the second is based on the vagrancy expeditions around London through which he gathered material. Orwell finished a first version in October 1930, with only the Paris material.

fuentes/sin-blanca-en-paris-y-londres/po.texto: It was aimed at middle- and upper-class readers, the most likely to be well educated, and it exposes the poverty that existed in two prosperous cities. In the introduction to the 1935 French edition, Orwell wrote that he had exaggerated nothing, except to the extent that every writer exaggerates when selecting.

fuentes/los-dias-de-birmania/resumen.texto: Orwell's first novel, published in 1934 and set in British Burma in the 1920s, in the fictional district of Kyauktada, based on Katha, where Orwell served as an imperial policeman. Its protagonist is John Flory, a lonely man trapped in a larger system, in what has been called a portrait of the dark side of the British Raj. Orwell drafted it in Paris between 1928 and 1929, revised it in 1932 in Southwold, and typed the final version in December 1933. Gollancz rejected it for fear of a libel suit, and Harper & Brothers published it first in the United States, in 1934; Gollancz issued the British edition on June 24, 1935.

fuentes/los-dias-de-birmania/por_que_imp.texto: It is a novel about the end of the British Empire, based on Orwell's own experience as a policeman in Burma.

fuentes/que-no-muera-la-aspidistra/resum.texto: Orwell's third novel, set in London in the 1930s. It tells of the romantic ambition of Gordon Comstock, a poet who defies the cult of money and status and for that reason leads a gloomy life. Orwell wrote it in 1934 and 1935, while living in various places near Hampstead and working in a second-hand bookshop, Booklovers' Corner, and Gollancz published it on April 20, 1936.

fuentes/que-no-muera-la-aspidistra/por_q.texto: Orwell later disparaged it: in a 1946 letter he wrote that it was one of the few books he was ashamed of, because he wrote it “as an exercise” and was forced to publish it out of need for money.

fuentes/cronicas-marcianas/resumen.texto: Science fiction novel assembled from previously published stories (what is called a fix-up in English) about the exploration and colonization of Mars, home to native Martians, by Americans who leave an Earth in crisis, devastated at the end by a nuclear war. Doubleday's representatives suggested to Bradbury in 1949 that he join his stories together, and the book came out in 1950; in the United Kingdom it was published in 1951 as The Silver Locusts. A 1997 edition moved the dates of the book's future forward by thirty-one years; in the first edition it ran from 1999 to 2026.

fuentes/cronicas-marcianas/por_que_impor.texto: It projects postwar American society onto a technological future, in which humanity's capacity to create and to destroy has miraculous and devastating consequences. Bradbury said that, on reading Sherwood Anderson's Winesburg, Ohio, he wanted to write a book as good as that one but set on Mars.

fuentes/el-vino-del-estio/resumen.texto: Novel from 1957 set in the summer of 1928 in Green Town, a fictional town in Illinois based on Waukegan, where Bradbury spent his childhood. Its protagonist is Douglas Spaulding, a twelve-year-old boy. It grew out of a story, “Dandelion Wine,” which appeared in Gourmet in June 1953; many chapters had been published earlier as separate stories, the first in 1946 and the others between 1950 and 1957. The dandelion wine the protagonist's grandfather makes is a metaphor for distilling the joys of summer.

fuentes/el-vino-del-estio/por_que_import.texto: It is the first book of the Green Town trilogy. In 2006 Bradbury published a sequel, Farewell Summer.

fuentes/historia-de-la-locura-en-la-epoc.texto: Michel Foucault's first major work, published in 1961: it examines how the meaning of madness changed in the cultures, laws, politics, philosophy and medicine of Europe, from the Middle Ages to the late eighteenth century, and criticizes the concept of mental illness. It begins in the Middle Ages and with how lepers were removed from the company of the healthy. He wrote it between 1955 and 1959, while holding cultural and teaching posts in Poland, Germany and Sweden, where he directed a French cultural centre at Uppsala University.

It is a critique of the idea of history and of the historical method. The philosopher José Guilherme Merquior argued in 1985 that factual and interpretive errors reduce the book's value as intellectual history.

fuentes/las-palabras-y-las-cosas/resumen.texto: 1966 book in which Foucault proposes that each historical period has underlying epistemic assumptions, or epistemes, which determine what is true and what discourse is acceptable, and studies them through the origins of biology, economics and linguistics. He distinguishes the episteme of the Renaissance, based on resemblance, that of the Classical age, based on representation and order, and that of Modernity, from Kant onward. Its introduction analyzes Velázquez's Las Meninas (1656).

fuentes/las-palabras-y-las-cosas/por_que.texto: It establishes the concept of episteme, central to Foucault's archaeology of knowledge. Foucault would have preferred to title it The Order of Things.

fuentes/historia-de-la-sexualidad/resume.texto: Four-volume study of sexuality in the Western world, in which Foucault examines how “sexuality” emerged as an object of discourse and as a sphere separate from life, and argues that the idea that every individual has a sexuality is relatively recent. The first volume, The Will to Knowledge, dates from 1976 and focuses on the last two centuries; The Use of Pleasure and The Care of the Self came out in 1984, the year of his death, and the work was left unfinished. The fourth, Confessions of the Flesh, was published posthumously in 2018, although Foucault had forbidden the posthumous publication of his works.

fuentes/historia-de-la-sexualidad/por_qu.texto: It proposes that sexuality is not a natural given but something that arose historically as an object of discourse.

fuentes/las-puertas-de-la-percepcion/res.texto: Autobiographical book in which Huxley recounts the mescaline experience he had in May 1953 at his home in West Hollywood, with the psychiatrist Humphry Osmond, and reflects on its philosophical and psychological implications, from purely aesthetic vision to “sacramental vision.” It was published in 1954, and the title and style come from William Blake. In 1956 he published a complementary essay, Heaven and Hell.

fuentes/las-puertas-de-la-percepcion/por.texto: It provoked strong reactions. Huxley continued taking psychedelics for the rest of his life, and that experience influenced his last novel, Island (1962).

fuentes/la-isla/resumen.texto: Utopian novel and manifesto published in 1962, Huxley's last novel. It tells the story of Will Farnaby, a cynical journalist who is shipwrecked on Pala, a fictional island. The plot serves mainly to develop ideas rather than to resolve a conventional narrative tension.

fuentes/la-isla/por_que_importa.texto: It is the utopian counterpoint to Brave New World (1932). The novel's ideas already appear in the preface Huxley wrote in 1946 for a new edition of that book.

fuentes/pabellon-del-cancer/resumen.texto: Semi-autobiographical novel about a small group of patients in Ward 13, the cancer ward, of a hospital in Tashkent, in Soviet Uzbekistan, during a few weeks in the spring of 1955, two years after Stalin's death. Its protagonist is Oleg Kostoglotov, a former Gulag prisoner. Solzhenitsyn finished it in mid-1966 and sent it in June to the magazine Novy Mir; that year it circulated in samizdat and the following year it was banned in the Soviet Union. In 1968 several European publishers issued it in Russian, and in April excerpts appeared in English without authorization in the Times Literary Supplement.

fuentes/pabellon-del-cancer/por_que_impo.texto: It circulated in the Soviet Union in clandestine copies while the regime banned it, and became known abroad through Russian editions and English excerpts.

fuentes/el-libro-de-los-gatos-habilidoso.texto: Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats

Collection of humorous, whimsical poems about the psychology and sociology of cats. Eliot wrote them in the 1930s and included them, signed with his nickname “Old Possum,” in letters to his godchildren. Faber and Faber gathered and published them in 1939, with illustrations by the author on the cover, and in 1940 reissued them with drawings by Nicolas Bentley.
It is the basis of the musical Cats, by Andrew Lloyd Webber, which premiered in 1981. According to The Guardian, critics in 1939 felt that Eliot had misjudged the mood of the country.

fuentes/final-de-partida/resumen.texto: Absurdist, tragicomic play in one act, originally written in French, which Beckett translated into English himself (Endgame). Its characters are Hamm, a blind, paralyzed and domineering old man, his elderly parents and his servant Clov, who await an “end” that is not specified, in an abandoned house in a post-apocalyptic landscape. It premiered in French on April 3, 1957, at the Royal Court Theatre in London, after accepting an invitation from George Devine, and was published that same year.

fuentes/final-de-partida/por_que_importa.texto: It is dedicated to Roger Blin, the director who had premiered Waiting for Godot in Paris and who, according to accounts, unsuccessfully sought a theatre in that city. Together with Waiting for Godot, it is considered one of Beckett's major works.

fuentes/ojos-azules/resumen.texto: Toni Morrison's first novel, published in 1970 and set in Lorain (Ohio), her hometown, in the early 1940s. It tells the story of Pecola Breedlove, a Black girl whom her surroundings consider “ugly” because of her features and her dark skin, and who as a result develops an inferiority complex. It is narrated mainly by Claudia MacTeer, the daughter of the family that takes in Pecola, with some passages from an omniscient third-person narrator.

fuentes/ojos-azules/por_que_importa.texto: Later analyses highlight its critique of white beauty standards, contrasted with Black ones, and of the “colonization of the mind.” It caused controversy because of its themes, and Morrison received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1993.

fuentes/finnegans-wake/resumen.texto: Novel published in fragments from 1924 under the title “Work in Progress,” and as a book on May 4, 1939, when its definitive title was revealed. Joyce wrote it in Paris over seventeen years: on March 10, 1923, he told his patron Harriet Shaw Weaver that he had written two pages, the first since the final “yes” of Ulysses. Its English is altered with words from many languages, and some commentators believe Joyce tried in this way to reproduce how memories, people and places blend together in a dream state.

fuentes/finnegans-wake/por_que_importa.texto: Its initial reception was largely negative. It has a reputation as one of the most difficult works in English-language literature to understand.

fuentes/retrato-del-artista-adolescente/.texto: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man

James Joyce's first novel, published in book form in 1916: a Künstlerroman in modernist style about the religious and intellectual awakening of Stephen Dedalus, the author's alter ego. It grew out of “Stephen Hero,” a realistic, autobiographical novel that Joyce began on February 2, 1904, and abandoned in September 1907, when he began to rewrite the text entirely. Ezra Pound had it serialized in the magazine The Egoist in 1914 and 1915.
With Dubliners (1914), it placed Joyce at the forefront of literary modernism.

fuentes/mientras-agonizo/resumen.texto: Southern Gothic novel of 1930, Faulkner's fifth, narrated by fifteen characters in 59 chapters, with interior monologue and chapters of varying length. It recounts the death of Addie Bundren and the journey of her poor, rural family to bury her. It is set in the fictional Yoknapatawpha County, in Mississippi. Faulkner said he wrote it in six weeks, without changing a word, while working nights as a fireman at the University of Mississippi's power plant. The title comes from the Odyssey in William Marris's 1925 translation.

fuentes/mientras-agonizo/por_que_importa.texto: Together with The Sound and the Fury, it is one of Faulkner's most studied novels.

fuentes/el-hobbit/resumen.texto: Children's fantasy novel that follows Bilbo Baggins, a homebody hobbit who joins the wizard Gandalf and the thirteen dwarves of Thorin's Company to reclaim the dwarves' home and treasure, held by the dragon Smaug. Tolkien recalled, in a 1955 letter to W. H. Auden, that he began it one day in the early 1930s, and by late 1932 had finished the tale; other chronologies have him beginning it in the late 1920s. Allen & Unwin published it on September 21, 1937.

fuentes/el-hobbit/por_que_importa.texto: It was nominated for the Carnegie Medal and won a New York Herald Tribune prize for best children's fiction. It is set in Middle-earth, the same world as The Lord of the Rings, and has sold more than 100 million copies.

fuentes/de-ratones-y-hombres/resumen.texto: Short novel of 1937 about George Milton and Lennie Small, two migrant ranch workers who travel through California looking for work during the Great Depression. Steinbeck based it on his experiences as a teenager working alongside migrant farm laborers in the 1910s, before the arrival of the “Okies” he would portray in The Grapes of Wrath. The title comes from a poem by Robert Burns, “To a Mouse.” It was adapted for the stage, premiering on May 21, 1937, less than three months after the novel, and for film in 1939.

fuentes/de-ratones-y-hombres/por_que_imp.texto: It is one of Steinbeck's best-known works, and it has been the target of repeated calls for censorship since its publication.

fuentes/despues-remarque/resumen.texto: Novel (also translated as The Road Back) generally considered the sequel to All Quiet on the Western Front. It follows other characters, although it can be assumed they were in the same company, and Tjaden is the only member of the 2nd Company who appears in both books. It takes place a few weeks after the end of the previous one and deals with the fall of the German Empire and the experience of young men returning from the trenches of World War I who try to readjust to civilian life. It was serialized in the newspaper Vossische Zeitung between December 1930 and January 1931, and published as a book in April 1931.

fuentes/despues-remarque/por_que_importa.texto: It returns to the world of the novel that had made Remarque famous in 1929, now in the postwar period.

personas/proust/resumen.texto: French novelist. He devoted his last fifteen years to In Search of Lost Time, whose second volume won the Prix Goncourt in 1919.

personas/joyce/resumen.texto: Irish writer who lived almost all his adult life outside Ireland, in Trieste, Zurich and Paris. With Ulysses and Finnegans Wake he took experimentation with interior monologue and language to the extreme.

personas/kafka/resumen.texto: Jewish writer from Prague who wrote in German, an employee of a workers’ accident insurance institute. He published little in his lifetime and asked his friend Max Brod to burn his manuscripts; Brod did not do so and edited his novels after his death.

personas/thomas-mann/resumen.texto: German novelist, Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929. An opponent of Nazism, he went into exile in 1933 in Switzerland and later in the United States, from where he spoke to Germans by radio during the war.

personas/virginia-woolf/resumen.texto: English novelist and essayist of the Bloomsbury Group and founder, with her husband Leonard, of the Hogarth Press. Her essay A Room of One’s Own (1929) is a central text of literary feminism.

personas/faulkner/resumen.texto: American novelist who set almost all his work in the imaginary Yoknapatawpha County, in Mississippi. Nobel Prize in Literature in 1949.

personas/hemingway/resumen.texto: American novelist and journalist, a correspondent in the Spanish Civil War and in the Second World War. Nobel Prize in Literature in 1954; he lived for twenty years in Cuba.

personas/orwell/resumen.texto: Pen name of Eric Arthur Blair, a British writer born in India. He fought in the Spanish Civil War in the POUM militias and from then on wrote against totalitarianism from the standpoint of democratic socialism.

personas/huxley/resumen.texto: English writer from a family of scientists. He settled in California in 1937 and in his last years wrote about mysticism and psychedelic drugs (The Doors of Perception, 1954).

personas/bradbury/resumen.texto: American writer of science fiction and fantasy, author of The Martian Chronicles (1950) and Fahrenheit 451.

personas/eliot/resumen.texto: Poet born in the United States who settled in England and became a British citizen in 1927. Nobel Prize in Literature in 1948.

personas/beckett/resumen.texto: Irish writer who lived in France and wrote in English and French. Nobel Prize in Literature in 1969.

personas/steinbeck/resumen.texto: American novelist of rural California and of the poor workers of the Great Depression. Nobel Prize in Literature in 1962.

personas/hesse/resumen.texto: German writer, a naturalized Swiss citizen from 1924, who lived in Montagnola from 1919. Nobel Prize in Literature in 1946; his novels were widely read by the counterculture of the 1960s.

personas/remarque/resumen.texto: German writer who fought on the Western Front in 1917. The Nazis burned his books and stripped him of his citizenship; he lived in exile in Switzerland and the United States.

personas/tolkien/resumen.texto: English philologist, professor of Anglo-Saxon and of English literature at Oxford. He invented languages and a complete mythology for Middle-earth, the setting of The Hobbit (1937) and The Lord of the Rings.

personas/nabokov/resumen.texto: Russian writer exiled after the revolution, who wrote in Russian in Berlin and in English in the United States, where he taught at Cornell University. He was also an entomologist specializing in butterflies.

personas/kundera/resumen.texto: Czech novelist. His books were banned in Czechoslovakia after the Prague Spring; he settled in France in 1975, lost his Czech citizenship in 1979 and from the 1990s wrote in French.

personas/saramago/resumen.texto: Portuguese novelist and Communist Party member. Nobel Prize in Literature in 1998, the first for a Portuguese-language author; from 1993 he lived in Lanzarote.

personas/garcia-lorca/resumen.texto: Andalusian poet and playwright of the Generation of ’27. He was shot by the rebels in August 1936, at the start of the Spanish Civil War; his remains have not been found.

personas/ernaux/resumen.texto: French writer who narrates her own life as a social document on class, gender and memory. Nobel Prize in Literature in 2022.

personas/pasternak/resumen.texto: Russian poet and novelist. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1958 and, faced with the Soviet government’s campaign against him, declined it.

personas/bulgakov/resumen.texto: Russian writer born in Kiev, a physician by training. His works were censored in the Soviet Union, and his major novel was published twenty-six years after his death.

personas/solzhenitsyn/resumen.texto: Russian writer, an officer in the Second World War and a prisoner in the Gulag from 1945 to 1953 for criticizing Stalin in a letter. Nobel Prize in Literature in 1970, he was expelled from the USSR in 1974 and returned to Russia in 1994.

personas/alexievich/resumen.texto: Belarusian journalist and writer who builds her books from hundreds of oral testimonies about the Soviet experience. Nobel Prize in Literature in 2015; an opponent of Lukashenko’s government, she left Belarus in 2020.

personas/krasznahorkai/resumen.texto: Hungarian novelist of long sentences and apocalyptic themes, several of whose works Béla Tarr adapted for the screen. Nobel Prize in Literature in 2025.

personas/primo-levi/resumen.texto: Italian Jewish chemist from Turin. An anti-fascist partisan, he was deported to Auschwitz in 1944 and survived; he devoted his work to bearing witness to the camp.

personas/ana-frank/resumen.texto: German Jewish girl whose family took refuge in Amsterdam. She hid with them from 1942 until they were discovered in August 1944; she died of typhus in the Bergen-Belsen camp.

personas/elie-wiesel/resumen.texto: Jewish writer born in Sighet (Romania), a survivor of Auschwitz and Buchenwald. Nobel Peace Prize in 1986 for his work on the memory of the Holocaust.

personas/tagore/resumen.texto: Bengali poet, musician and educator. In 1913 he became the first non-European author to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature; he composed the songs that are today the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.

personas/kawabata/resumen.texto: Japanese novelist. In 1968 he became the first Japanese person to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature.

personas/mahfuz/resumen.texto: Egyptian novelist, a civil servant for decades. Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988, the first for an author writing in Arabic; in 1994 he survived a stabbing by an Islamist who accused him of blasphemy.

personas/achebe/resumen.texto: Nigerian novelist of Igbo ethnicity. His critique of the image of Africa in Conrad’s Heart of Darkness (1975) opened a central debate in postcolonial studies.

personas/rushdie/resumen.texto: British novelist born in Bombay. From 1989 he lived under the threat of an Iranian fatwa ordering his killing; in 2022 he was stabbed in New York State and lost an eye.

personas/pamuk/resumen.texto: Turkish novelist from Istanbul. Nobel Prize in Literature in 2006; in 2005 he was prosecuted for “insulting Turkish identity” after mentioning the Armenian genocide in an interview, and the case was dropped.

personas/han-kang/resumen.texto: South Korean novelist born in Gwangju. Nobel Prize in Literature in 2024, the first time it was awarded to a Korean author and to an Asian woman.

personas/toni-morrison/resumen.texto: American novelist who wrote about the history and life of African Americans. Nobel Prize in Literature in 1993, the first Black woman to receive it.

personas/rodo/resumen.texto: Uruguayan essayist and deputy, a figure of modernismo. His Ariel offered Spanish American youth an ideal of culture as opposed to the utilitarianism he attributed to the United States.

personas/jose-ingenieros/resumen.texto: Psychiatrist and sociologist born in Palermo (Italy) and raised in Buenos Aires. A socialist in his youth, he was among the authors most read by the students of the University Reform of 1918.

personas/vasconcelos/resumen.texto: Mexican philosopher and politician, rector of the National University and Secretary of Public Education from 1921 to 1924, when he promoted literacy campaigns and the murals. In 1929 he ran for president and denounced fraud.

personas/gabriela-mistral/resumen.texto: Pen name of Lucila Godoy Alcayaga, a rural schoolteacher, poet and Chilean consul. In 1945 she became the first person from Latin America to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature.

personas/ortega-y-gasset/resumen.texto: Spanish philosopher, founder of the Revista de Occidente (1923). He visited Argentina in 1916 and 1928 and lived there from 1939 to 1942; he had a great influence on Argentine thought.

personas/victoria-ocampo/resumen.texto: Argentine writer and editor, founder of the magazine and publishing house Sur. She was the first woman in the Academia Argentina de Letras (1977).

personas/borges/resumen.texto: Argentine writer, director of the Biblioteca Nacional from 1955 to 1973. His stories of labyrinths, mirrors and libraries influenced world literature; he never received the Nobel, for which he was a candidate for many years.

personas/arlt/resumen.texto: Argentine novelist, playwright and journalist, the son of immigrants. His Aguafuertes porteñas in the newspaper El Mundo portrayed the Buenos Aires of the 1930s.

personas/bioy-casares/resumen.texto: Argentine writer, friend and co-author of Borges and husband of Silvina Ocampo. 1990 Cervantes Prize.

personas/sabato/resumen.texto: Argentine physicist and writer who left science for literature. He chaired CONADEP, which in 1984 delivered the Nunca más report on the disappeared of the dictatorship.

personas/cortazar/resumen.texto: Argentine writer born in Brussels, who lived in Paris from 1951 and became a French citizen in 1981. A master of the fantastic short story (Bestiario, 1951) and a figure of the Latin American Boom.

personas/miguel-angel-asturias/resumen.texto: Guatemalan writer who studied Maya culture in Paris and lived through long exiles, including in Argentina. 1967 Nobel Prize in Literature.

personas/neruda/resumen.texto: Pen name of Ricardo Eliécer Neftalí Reyes Basoalto, Chilean poet, consul and Communist senator. 1971 Nobel Prize in Literature; he died days after the 1973 coup, in circumstances that the Chilean courts investigated on suspicion of poisoning.

personas/octavio-paz/resumen.texto: Mexican poet and essayist. He resigned his post as ambassador to India after the 1968 Tlatelolco massacre; 1990 Nobel Prize in Literature.

personas/rulfo/resumen.texto: Mexican writer and photographer from Jalisco. His work fits in two books, The Burning Plain (1953) and Pedro Páramo.

personas/garcia-marquez/resumen.texto: Colombian novelist and journalist who lived in Mexico City from 1961. 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature and a central figure of magical realism.

personas/vargas-llosa/resumen.texto: Peruvian novelist, also a naturalized Spanish citizen. A candidate for president of Peru in 1990, he lost to Alberto Fujimori; he moved from socialism to liberalism. 2010 Nobel Prize in Literature.

personas/husserl/resumen.texto: German philosopher born in Moravia, founder of phenomenology. Because of his Jewish origin, the Nazi regime barred him from teaching and publishing in his final years.

personas/freud/resumen.texto: Jewish physician and neurologist from Vienna, creator of psychoanalysis. He fled to London after the annexation of Austria by Nazi Germany in 1938 and died there a year later.

personas/bertrand-russell/resumen.texto: British philosopher, logician and mathematician, one of the founders of analytic philosophy. A pacifist imprisoned during the First World War and an activist against nuclear weapons; 1950 Nobel Prize in Literature.

personas/whitehead/resumen.texto: English mathematician and philosopher, Russell's teacher at Cambridge. From 1924 he taught at Harvard, where he developed process philosophy.

personas/wittgenstein/resumen.texto: Austrian philosopher from a family of Viennese industrialists, a student of Russell at Cambridge. He wrote two works that read as two different philosophies and taught at Cambridge between 1929 and 1947.

personas/heidegger/resumen.texto: German philosopher, a student of Husserl. He joined the Nazi Party in 1933 as rector of the University of Freiburg; the publication of his Black Notebooks from 2014 onward rekindled the debate over his antisemitism.

personas/sartre/resumen.texto: French philosopher and writer, the central figure of existentialism and partner of Simone de Beauvoir. He was an intellectual committed to the left and declined the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1964.

personas/camus/resumen.texto: French writer born in Algeria to a poor family. He edited the Resistance newspaper Combat and broke with Sartre in 1952 over his criticism of Soviet communism; 1957 Nobel Prize in Literature, he died in a car accident.

personas/foucault/resumen.texto: French philosopher and historian, professor at the Collège de France from 1970. He studied how knowledge and power are intertwined in madness, medicine, prison and sexuality.

personas/derrida/resumen.texto: French philosopher born in Algeria, creator of deconstruction. Highly influential in literary theory at American universities and widely criticized by analytic philosophy.

personas/habermas/resumen.texto: German philosopher and sociologist of the second generation of the Frankfurt School. He theorized the public sphere and communicative reason and took part in the major public debates of postwar Germany.

personas/kuhn/resumen.texto: American physicist, historian and philosopher of science. He taught at Harvard, Berkeley, Princeton and MIT.

personas/rawls/resumen.texto: American political philosopher, professor at Harvard from 1962. He renewed liberal political philosophy with the idea of justice as fairness.

personas/durkheim/resumen.texto: French sociologist, the son of a rabbi, regarded as one of the founders of sociology as an academic discipline. He taught in Bordeaux and, from 1902, at the Sorbonne.

personas/max-weber/resumen.texto: German sociologist, economist and historian, one of the founders of sociology. He studied the rationalization of modern life, bureaucracy and the relationship between religion and economy.

personas/saussure/resumen.texto: Swiss linguist, professor in Geneva. His ideas on language as a system of signs, known through a posthumous book, founded structural linguistics.

personas/bernays/resumen.texto: American publicist born in Vienna, nephew of Sigmund Freud, regarded as the father of public relations. He worked for companies and governments, including United Fruit in the 1954 Guatemalan coup.

personas/levi-strauss/resumen.texto: French anthropologist, creator of structural anthropology. He taught in São Paulo and studied Indigenous peoples of Brazil between 1935 and 1939.

personas/mcluhan/resumen.texto: Canadian communication theorist, professor at the University of Toronto. He coined “the medium is the message” and “the global village”.

personas/chomsky/resumen.texto: American linguist, professor at MIT, creator of generative grammar. He is also a well-known left-wing critic of US foreign policy and of the mainstream media.

personas/alfred-nobel/resumen.texto: Swedish chemist and industrialist, inventor of dynamite. In his 1895 will he left most of his fortune to create the prizes that bear his name.

hechos/primeros-premios-nobel/lugar.texto: Royal Swedish Academy of Music, Stockholm

hechos/primeros-premios-nobel/resumen.texto: On 10 December 1901, the fifth anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death, the first prizes in physics, chemistry, medicine and literature were awarded in Stockholm, and the peace prize in Christiania (Oslo), in accordance with the will of the inventor of dynamite. The first Nobel Prize in Literature went to the French poet Sully Prudhomme rather than to Tolstoy, which prompted protests from Swedish writers. Since then it has been the most visible international consecration for a writer.

hechos/fallo-sobre-el-ulises/titulo.texto: A New York judge rules that Ulysses is not obscene

hechos/fallo-sobre-el-ulises/resumen.texto: On 6 December 1933 federal judge John M. Woolsey ruled, in a case sought by the publisher Random House, that Joyce's Ulysses was not obscene and could enter the United States, where customs seized copies. The Court of Appeals upheld the ruling in 1934, by two votes to one, and Random House published the book that year. It was a central precedent against the censorship of literary works.

hechos/quema-de-libros-de-1933/resumen.texto: On 10 May 1933, shortly after Hitler came to power, Nazi students burned more than twenty thousand books in Berlin's Opernplatz, with a speech by Joseph Goebbels, and similar burnings took place in other university towns. Works by Jewish, Marxist and pacifist authors, or by those deemed “anti-German”, went up in flames, such as Marx, Freud, Heinrich Mann, Erich Kästner and Remarque. A memorial by Micha Ullman, an empty library beneath the square's pavement, commemorates the event.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-revista-sur/titul.texto: Victoria Ocampo founds the magazine Sur

hechos/fundacion-de-la-revista-sur/resum.texto: In 1931 Victoria Ocampo founded the magazine Sur in Buenos Aires, adding in 1933 a publishing house of the same name. For four decades it spread European and North American literature and thought in Argentina, with translations of authors such as Virginia Woolf, a friend of Ocampo's, and published Argentine writers such as Borges, Bioy Casares and Sabato. Its critics accused it of being elitist and foreign-oriented, and Peronism saw it as an organ of the liberal opposition.

hechos/nobel-a-gabriela-mistral/titulo.texto: Gabriela Mistral, Latin America's first Nobel Prize in Literature

hechos/nobel-a-gabriela-mistral/resumen.texto: In November 1945 the Swedish Academy awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature to the Chilean poet Gabriela Mistral, the first person from Latin America to receive it and the fifth woman. She received it in Stockholm on 10 December of that year.

hechos/pasternak-rechaza-el-nobel/titulo.texto: Pasternak forced to renounce the Nobel

hechos/pasternak-rechaza-el-nobel/resume.texto: On 23 October 1958 the Swedish Academy announced the Nobel Prize in Literature for Boris Pasternak, who accepted it by telegram. The Soviet government and the Writers' Union launched a campaign against him, expelled him from the Union and threatened him with exile, and a few days later Pasternak renounced the prize. His son received the medal in Stockholm in 1989.

hechos/sartre-rechaza-el-nobel/resumen.texto: In October 1964 the Swedish Academy awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature to Jean-Paul Sartre, who declined it in a public statement. He explained that he had always refused official honors because a writer should not allow himself to be turned into an institution, and that in the midst of the Cold War the prize favored Western writers and dissidents from the East.

hechos/boom-latinoamericano/resumen.texto: A publishing and literary phenomenon of the 1960s and early 1970s in which the novels of Cortázar, García Márquez, Vargas Llosa and Carlos Fuentes, among others, reached a mass readership in Latin America and around the world. Its publishing centers were Barcelona, with the publisher Seix Barral and the literary agent Carmen Balcells, and Buenos Aires, with Sudamericana. The Cuban Revolution was at first a common cause for the group, which split in 1971 over the arrest of the Cuban poet Heberto Padilla.

hechos/fatua-contra-rushdie/resumen.texto: On 14 February 1989 Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, the leader of Iran, issued a fatwa sentencing to death Salman Rushdie and everyone involved in publishing The Satanic Verses, on the grounds that the novel offended Islam, and an Iranian foundation offered a reward. Rushdie lived in hiding for years under police protection; the Japanese translator was murdered in 1991 and the Norwegian publisher was shot in 1993. In 2022 a young man stabbed him in New York State.

hechos/proceso-de-siniavski-y-daniel/res.texto: The writers Andrei Sinyavsky and Yuli Daniel, arrested in September 1965, were tried in Moscow in February 1966 before the Moscow City Court, presided over by Lev Smirnov, for “anti-Soviet agitation and propaganda” (Article 70 of the RSFSR Criminal Code, which was applied for the first time to works of fiction) for publishing their satires of Soviet life abroad, under the pseudonyms Abram Terz and Nikolai Arzhak. They pleaded not guilty, something unusual in a political case, and were sentenced to seven and five years in labor camps; Sinyavsky was released in 1971, after serving six years. It was the first Soviet trial in which writers were openly sentenced solely for their work, and it is usually seen as the end of Khrushchev's thaw. The Supreme Court of the RSFSR overturned the sentence in 1991.

hechos/expulsion-de-solzhenitsyn/resumen.texto: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, expelled from the Writers' Union in 1969 and winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1970 (he did not travel to Stockholm for fear of not being allowed to return), was arrested on February 12, 1974, and deported the next day to Frankfurt, in West Germany, stripped of his Soviet citizenship. The KGB had found a manuscript of The Gulag Archipelago; the Politburo, guided by KGB chief Yuri Andropov, chose expulsion to a country that would accept him after a statement by Chancellor Willy Brandt.
